chunks.text: Where do people go? If you're moved on from everywhere, there is nowhere to be. Death from homelessness. Caitlin died at 47, ill, rundown, and fatigued after having to sleep outside in Christchurch in late autumn 2025 from two respiratory infections, including the common cold because of her lifelong immunosuppression to prevent her kidney transplant rejecting.

Caitlin's previous hospital renal specialist concluded in his report I provided the coroner, "With suitable and stable housing, Caitlin should have had many years of life ahead of her with a functioning transplant." Her death was entirely preventable, but inevitable given the failures of those with a duty of care, MSD, Ministry of Social Development, Public Trust, the health system, and New Zealand Police.

Caitlin was brave, ethical, articulate, and persevering. She stood up for herself. People found that difficult. Caitlin lived in miserable, unhealthy, and unsafe conditions, sleeping in parks until moved on or abused by neighbors, in derelict houses, or taken in by people who professed to help her but preyed on her.

She was abused, attacked, assaulted, and stolen from repeatedly. My daughter survived less than two years homeless, dying at half the age of both her grandmothers. Homeless people die 30 years early. Caitlin wrote that the previous year hospital told her that if she continued to live outdoors in winter, she would not survive to spring.

Family and others slept in that winter. As recent New Zealand research finds, homeless people die 30 years earlier than the rest of us with a roof over our heads. And to quote from that report, "Premature mortality results from a complex combination of medical conditions, often related to severe and chronic comorbidities, and the consequences of social exclusion shaped by homelessness." That is marginalization and stigma, loneliness, violence, and adverse living conditions.

That's what the move on orders will do even more. MSD refused Caitlin housing. Caitlin was not provided a permanent home, despite MSD assessing her as A20, the top of the social housing wait list, nor did MSD provide her with emergency housing for more than a year.

I am now walking in Caitlin's shoes, experiencing the same rejection and runaround, showing how difficult it is to navigate a fragmented, unresponsive, and unaccountable system, then and now. Caitlin had no chance. Now we know that MSD has incentives for managers and staff to turn down emergency housing, meeting government targets set in 2024 five years early.

Even more shockingly, I found out that MSD does not have to consider whether declining emergency housing would, in quotes, "Increase or create any risk to the welfare or life of the applicant." Public Trust then rejected her GP certification in February 2025 that Caitlin was at serious and imminent risk of death to enable her to withdraw her $48,000 KiwiSaver to be safely housed and cared for without taking any medical advice at all.

She was found dead three months later after having to sleep outside in late autumn. Move on orders push homeless people to the margins away from support. Move on orders risk pushing people further away from housing, outreach support services, trusted relationships, vital health services, and basic public amenities such as showers, toilets, and lockers.

Caitlin's GP and pharmacy were in central Christchurch, as was WINZ, the food bank, and other support services, and the library where she spent her days in a warm, safe environment with free Wi-Fi. Police did not protect Caitlin as she expected, instead arresting her, including during welfare checks. That is, Caitlin was already criminalized, homeless, never having been in trouble with police before.

Police did not refer her to housing as government states is the police role when issuing move on orders. Police themselves oppose this. Police did not even ensure she was safe when assisting her to leave yet another unsuitable place with a 24 hours safety order the weekend before she was found dead in the same flat she had returned on her own solely to collect her warm gear, it being cold.

Instead of moving homeless people to the margins, police need to be required to refer rough sleepers to a home, together with connecting them with the help and other support they need. Moving on homelessness. As the Auditor-General recommends in his March 2026 report, Supporting People in Immediate Housing Need, a joined up government response is essential to make real progress in reducing the extent of homelessness and unstable housing.

The proposed move on orders do the opposite. A duty to assist is needed instead. We need an integrated approach, listening to those who know, across party and across government. To end, my beautiful daughter. To end, Caitlin was my beautiful daughter.

Caitlin could be your daughter. She could be your sister, your friend, your cousin, your aunt. This could happen to any of us. Housing is a human right: decent, warm, affordable, secure housing. With a home, everything else can be sorted as the housing first approach Thank you.
